accuracy.evidence: The four roles match the topic's own description (leader, supporter, mediator, idea-generator) and the IB PYP PSPE Interactions outcomes on taking on roles in a group. The mediator definition (helps both sides state what they want and reach a solution both accept, without judging who is right) follows standard peer-mediation practice; the adult text notes that classroom role names vary (facilitator, recorder, timekeeper, encourager) rather than claiming one fixed set.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets three documented slips in primary group work: everyone competing to be leader (step 1 starts with four crowns and a stalled build; quiz tags fast and happy), the mediator acting as a judge (step 2 prediction, quiz tag judge, gap-step feedback) and supporting roles seen as lesser (step 4 prediction disproved when the supporter sits out and no planks go up; quiz tag only). Not getting your idea picked is handled by the sulk and push tags.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagroles is built on role badges handed to a team that all wear crowns, a stuck-team seat that only accepts the missing role, and a sit-out tap that removes one role and shows its specific failure on the treehouse. No other personal and social lab models a team's division of labour; flagteam teaches cooperate/compromise words with a log lift, and the shingle gate passed against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner sees the treehouse stay at zero planks while four friends say My way, and it fills only as each badge replaces a crown, so the one-leader rule is discovered before it is stated. Fixing the three stuck teams requires reading the problem and reasoning which job is absent, and the sit-out step shows that each role prevents a different failure, which is the key idea.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions each carry a tempting wrong option: four leaders being best, the peacemaker picking who is right, and the leader mattering most. Each is disproved inside its own step by the stalled build, by the matching card where the peacemaker lets Owl and Rabbit both speak, and by the empty treehouse when the supporter sits out; the done message then reports what the child predicted.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with ten tagged wrong answers (fast, happy, lead, peace, judge, walk, sulk, push, only, boss). Each says why that exact choice misses, for example that a peacemaker does not pick a winner but helps both sides find a fix, rather than a generic try again. In-lab drags also name the slip, such as giving a badge to a friend who already has a job or offering a role the team already has.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation scores FK grade 2.4 with short sentences and one role per sentence, each with a line the friend actually says. Adult text is grade 10.0, inside the family limit, and lists the key terms for ages 7 to 9. Lab cards are one short speech line, and every role carries an emoji badge plus its name.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph defines a role with a spoken example or shows what happens with too many leaders; adult paragraphs give curriculum placement, key terms, three named mistakes and what each lab step practises. Practice and mastery items each test identifying a role, a missing role or why a role matters, with no definition-copying items.

mobile.evidence: Checked screenshots at 360 px Android dark and iPhone 13 light for all six steps: four friend tiles fit in one row with names under them, the four role bins fit across the top, the sit-out message now sits on a card so it stays readable over the grass, and the button twins wrap onto full-width rows. Show me finished every task on the iPhone 13 profile in the browser gate.

accessibility.evidence: The browser gate's axe-core run found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark theme on desktop or iPhone 13, and logged no console errors. Every canvas action has a labelled button twin (give a badge, match a card, add a role, sit out, choose a role), and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with each result message. Roles are named in text as well as by emoji, so colour is never the only cue.
